title: Can a sealed class permit itself?
shortTitle: Can a sealed class permit itself?

s1_definition.profdef: No. A sealed class cannot list itself in its own `permits` clause. The `permits` clause names the *direct subtypes* allowed to extend the sealed type, and a type cannot be its own subtype — a class cannot extend itself. Attempting `sealed class Account permits Account` is a compile error because it is cyclic and meaningless. A sealed non-abstract class can itself be instantiated as a leaf, but that is different from permitting itself; it simply means the sealed class is concrete.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India's head office writes the closed list of products that may be "a kind of Account." Putting "Account" itself on that list makes no sense, because the list is meant to name the specific products that are types of Account, not the concept of Account repeating itself. A category cannot be a member of its own membership list — that is circular and empty of meaning. So head office never writes the concept's own name on the list of its approved variants.
s1_definition.oneliner: A sealed class cannot permit itself because `permits` lists direct subtypes, and nothing can be its own subtype.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** No. A sealed class cannot list itself in its own `permits` clause. The `permits` clause names the *direct subtypes* allowed to extend the sealed type, and a type cannot be its own subtype — a class cannot extend itself. Attempting `sealed class Account permits Account` is a compile error because it is cyclic and meaningless. A sealed non-abstract class can itself be instantiated as a leaf, but that is different from permitting itself; it simply means the sealed class is concrete.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India's head office writes the closed list of products that may be "a kind of Account." Putting "Account" itself on that list makes no sense, because the list is meant to name the specific products that are types of Account, not the concept of Account repeating itself. A category cannot be a member of its own membership list — that is circular and empty of meaning. So head office never writes the concept's own name on the list of its approved variants.

**One line to remember:** A sealed class cannot permit itself because `permits` lists direct subtypes, and nothing can be its own subtype.

sections.s2_technical:
The `permits` clause declares the set of **direct subtypes** that may extend or implement the sealed type. By definition a subtype is a *different* type that inherits from the sealed type. A class cannot extend itself — Java forbids a class being its own superclass, directly or through a cycle — so a sealed type can never appear in its own `permits` list. Writing `sealed class Account permits Account {}` produces a **compile error** about a cyclic or invalid permitted subtype, because `Account extends Account` is not a valid relationship.

This is sometimes confused with a related but different question: can a sealed class itself be a **concrete, instantiable type** that participates in the hierarchy as a value? The answer there is yes, but it has nothing to do with permitting itself. If a sealed class is **not abstract**, it can be instantiated directly, so the sealed class is itself a usable leaf value in addition to having permitted subclasses. For example `sealed class Node permits Branch {}` where `Node` is concrete means you can create a `Node` and also a `Branch`, but `Node` did not permit itself — it permitted `Branch`, and it is usable on its own because it is non-abstract.

Another nearby confusion is a **recursive data structure**, such as a tree where a node contains references to other nodes of the same sealed type. That is fine and common: the sealed type can have fields of its own type, and subtypes can reference the sealed supertype. Recursion in the data (a node holding child nodes) is completely different from a type permitting itself in its `permits` clause. The former is normal composition; the latter is an illegal inheritance cycle.

The rule also connects to how sealing is recorded. The permitted set goes into the `PermittedSubclasses` class-file attribute, listing the direct subclasses. The sealed class's own entry is never in that list because the attribute describes who may extend it, not the class itself. The JVM validates at load time that each permitted entry is a genuine direct subclass, and a self-reference would fail that validation just as it fails compilation.

A senior nuance is that this reflects a general principle: inheritance forms a **directed acyclic graph** rooted at `Object`, and any cycle, including a one-node self-cycle, is forbidden throughout Java, not just for sealed types. Another nuance is that if you want the sealed type to be usable as a value and also closed, you make it a **non-abstract sealed class** with permitted subtypes, which gives you a concrete base plus a closed set of specialisations, but you still never list the base in its own permits. A final nuance is that for modelling, if you find yourself wanting a type to permit itself, it usually signals you actually want either a concrete sealed base or a recursive field, and recognising that keeps the design clean in a banking domain model.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A developer at National Bank of India mistakenly tries to write a sealed `Account` that permits itself, thinking it would let `Account` be both the base and a usable value. We need to show this does not compile and explain why, so the team understands the rule.

Problem 2 — The actual goal was to have a concrete, usable base type alongside closed specialisations. The correct solution is a **non-abstract sealed class** that permits its real subtypes while being instantiable itself, which we demonstrate with a sealed `LedgerNode` that is concrete and permits a `SummaryNode`.

Problem 3 — The team also wants a recursive structure where a node references other nodes of the same type, which is often mistaken for self-permitting. We show a sealed `TransactionNode` holding a list of child `TransactionNode` values, proving recursion in data is fine and unrelated to permits.

In the mini-project we show, in comments, the illegal self-permit, then a correct concrete sealed base with a permitted subtype, and a correct recursive sealed structure, logging traversal results.

The code contains: a concrete sealed `LedgerNode` with a permitted `SummaryNode`, a recursive sealed `TransactionNode`, and a demo.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a concrete `LedgerNode` base, a `SummaryNode` subtype, and a recursive `TransactionNode` tree with a root over two leaves of 50,000 and 30,000.

Step 1 — The compiler rejects the illegal `sealed class Account permits Account` shown in comments, because a type cannot be its own subtype and inheritance cannot form a cycle. This is the direct answer to the question.

Step 2 — The code then creates a `LedgerNode` directly. This works because `LedgerNode` is a non-abstract sealed class, so it is itself an instantiable value, while still permitting the different subtype `SummaryNode`. This is the correct way to have a usable base, and it is not self-permitting.

Step 3 — A `SummaryNode` is created as the permitted final subtype. Both the base and the subtype describe themselves, showing the concrete base and its one permitted specialisation coexisting.

Step 4 — The code builds a recursive `TransactionNode` tree: two leaf nodes and a root that holds them as children of the same type. Calling `total` on the root recurses through the children, summing 0 plus 50,000 plus 30,000 to give 80,000. This proves that a type having fields of its own type is normal recursion, entirely different from permitting itself.

Step 5 — The results are logged, confirming the concrete base, the permitted subtype, and the recursive total all behave correctly without any self-permit.

```
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] Concrete base usable: LedgerNode LED-ROOT Rs.0
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] Permitted subtype:   SummaryNode LED-SUM Rs.1250000 children=2
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] Recursive total under root = Rs.80000
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ILLEGAL: sealed class Account permits Account {}
     └─ (Avoid) compile error: a type cannot be its own subtype (cycle)

  CORRECT 1 — concrete sealed base (NOT self-permit):
     sealed class LedgerNode permits SummaryNode   ← permits a DIFFERENT type
        │ non-abstract → base itself instantiable
        ├─ new LedgerNode(...)   usable value
        └─ final SummaryNode extends LedgerNode

  CORRECT 2 — recursive data (NOT self-permit):
     TransactionNode { amount; children: List<TransactionNode> }
        root(0)
         ├─ leaf1(50,000)
         └─ leaf2(30,000)
        total() = 0 + 50,000 + 30,000 = 80,000
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Self-Permit Is Illegal ═══

  ┌─ Rules ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ permits lists DIRECT SUBTYPES; a type is never its own subtype │
  │ `sealed X permits X` → compile error (inheritance cycle)       │
  │ concrete (non-abstract) sealed class = usable base + subtypes  │
  │ recursive field of same type = composition, perfectly legal    │
  │ inheritance graph is acyclic, rooted at Object                 │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────┐  permits (different type)
  │ <<sealed>> LedgerNode     │────────────────┐
  │ (non-abstract, usable)    │                │
  │ - id, amount              │                ▼
  │ + describe()              │     ┌──────────────────────────┐
  └──────────────────────────┘     │ SummaryNode (final)       │
                                    │ - childCount              │
                                    └──────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ TransactionNode (final)                   │
  │ - amount: BigDecimal                      │
  │ - children: List<TransactionNode>  ◆      │  recursive composition
  │ + total(): sum amount + children.total()  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Call Chain:
    1. new LedgerNode(...) → usable base
    2. new SummaryNode(...) → permitted subtype
    3. root.total() → 0 + 50,000 + 30,000 = 80,000
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
No, a sealed class cannot permit itself. The permits clause names the direct subtypes allowed to extend the sealed type, and by definition a subtype is a different type that inherits from it. A class cannot extend itself, and Java forbids any inheritance cycle, so writing a sealed Account that permits Account is a compile error about a cyclic or invalid permitted subtype. It is simply meaningless to list a type in its own list of variants.

There are two nearby ideas that people confuse with self-permitting, and I like to clear both up. The first is whether a sealed class can itself be a usable, instantiable value. That is yes, but it has nothing to do with permitting itself: if the sealed class is non-abstract, it can be instantiated directly, so it is a usable leaf in addition to having permitted subclasses. In my banking project I have a concrete sealed ledger node that is itself usable and permits a different summary-node subtype. The base is concrete, and it permits a different type, never itself.

The second confusion is a recursive data structure, like a tree where a node holds references to other nodes of the same type. That is completely normal composition and is legal. In my project a transaction node holds a list of child transaction nodes and sums them recursively. Having a field of your own type is recursion in the data, which is entirely different from a type appearing in its own permits clause.

The underlying principle I mention is that Java's inheritance forms a directed acyclic graph rooted at Object, so any cycle, including a one-node self-cycle, is forbidden everywhere, not only for sealed types. And practically, if I ever find myself wanting a type to permit itself, that is a signal I actually want either a concrete sealed base so the base is a usable value, or a recursive field to model a tree. Recognising which of those two I really need keeps the domain model clean, and neither one involves a type permitting itself.

keyPoints: sealed: restrict which classes can extend/implement
permits: explicit list of allowed subclasses
Subclass must be: final, sealed, or non-sealed
Enables exhaustive switch/pattern matching — compiler checks all cases
